# Diagnosing High Idle on the Holden Rodeo 6VE1

A common complaint for owners of the Holden Rodeo equipped with the 2.5L or 3.5L 6VE1 V6 engine is a persistent high idle, often settling around 2,000 rpm regardless of gear selection or load. This specific behavior usually manifests immediately after gasket replacement or an oil change, leading many to assume the issue lies in the ignition timing or fuel pressure before checking the air management system. When a smoke test confirms there are no external vacuum leaks, the fault is almost certainly internal to the engine's airflow control logic.

The most frequent culprit identified by mechanics in this scenario is the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve. The 6VE1 utilizes a stepper motor IAC valve that bypasses airflow around the throttle plate when the pedal is not depressed. The ECU modulates the motor steps to maintain the target idle speed, typically around 750â850 rpm in park or neutral. If the engine sits at 2,000 rpm after a cold start and remains there while warm, the IAC valve is either mechanically stuck in an open position, electrically shorted, or receiving incorrect duty cycle commands from the ECU.

Replacing the IAC valve is a logical first step, as carbon buildup can prevent the pintle from seating fully even on a new unit. However, simply swapping the part without verifying the electrical signal or cleaning the throttle body bore often results in a recurrence of the issue. The throttle body itself acts as an air metering device; if the idle speed control (ISC) port is clogged with oil residue from recent gasket work, the fresh air valve cannot bypass enough air to stabilize the engine, forcing the ECU to open the IAC fully to compensate. This creates a false reading of high airflow demand, resulting in the persistent 2,000 rpm idle.

Before condemning the entire intake system, verify the throttle position sensor (TPS). On the 6VE1, the TPS provides critical data on whether the pedal is depressed and the current throttle angle. If the TPS voltage drifts slightly upward at idle, the ECU interprets this as a light load or acceleration request, commanding a higher air volume to match the perceived demand. This mimics a high idle condition even when the throttle plate is physically closed. A multimeter check should show a steady voltage curve without sudden jumps or offsets that correlate with engine speed changes.

Another potential pitfall involves the electronic throttle control (ETC) calibration if the vehicle has been modified or repaired recently. Modern ECUs often require an adaptation procedure after replacing components that affect idle airflow. If the ECU does not learn the new baseline for the IAC and TPS combination, it may hold a "rich" fuel trim strategy to prevent stalling, which manifests as elevated RPMs. This is particularly common if the throttle body was cleaned but not recalibrated via the diagnostic port.

If you have access to an OBD-II scanner capable of reading live data streams, monitor the long-term and short-term fuel trims while at idle. Excessively positive fuel trims indicate the ECU is trying to compensate for a perceived vacuum leak or excessive airflow, confirming that the mechanical bypass air path is not sealing correctly. In some cases, the coolant temperature sensor may also be providing inaccurate data, telling the ECU the engine is cold when it is actually at operating temperature, causing the ECU to maintain high-idle enrichment indefinitely.

Addressing this issue requires a methodical approach: verify the mechanical seating of the IAC, ensure the throttle body bore is free of obstructions, check TPS voltage stability, and confirm that the ECU has adapted to the new hardware configuration. Ignoring these steps in favor of part replacement alone often wastes significant time and resources chasing a problem that lies in the interaction between sensors and actuators rather than a single failed component.
